opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most underappreciated parts of the whole picture. If you look at why ordinary people have had a decent share of the pie, at least in the last couple of centuries, a big part of the answer is that their labour was valuable and couldn't easily be done without. You needed workers to run the factories, staff the armies, pay the taxes and keep the bureaucracy going. That gave people bargaining power, both individually, because you could quit and work somewhere else, and collectively, because you could strike or organize or simply refuse to cooperate.

A lot of what we think of as liberal values, like broad education, public health and even the franchise, arguably got extended partly because states that invested in their people out-competed states that didn't. A healthy, educated, motivated population was a strategic asset. So there was a kind of convergence between what was good for people and what was good for the powerful institutions they lived inside.

If AI can do essentially all economically and militarily relevant work better and cheaper than any human, that convergence breaks. Your labour isn't worth much, so you can't bargain with it. A strike doesn't hurt anyone if the machines keep running. And the state's revenue doesn't depend on a thriving human tax base anymore. It might come from AI-driven production owned by a relatively small number of entities.

Then the question becomes: what's left to keep things equal? You still have capital, if you happen to own some, and that might grow a lot. But capital is already very unequally distributed, and when returns flow to whoever owns the machines, that inequality tends to compound. You could hope for redistribution, something like a UBI, but redistribution has always depended on the people asking for it having some leverage. If you're not needed, your claim rests on goodwill, on norms, on legal structures that were built when you were needed.

I don't want to say that leads inevitably to some dystopia. Norms and institutions can be sticky, and people do care about each other. But I'd say the default forces that pushed toward broad-based prosperity get much weaker, and we'd be relying on things that, historically, haven't been strong enough on their own. That's why I think it's worth thinking now about how to lock in protections, or create new sources of leverage, before our labour stops being the thing that keeps us in the game.

r001.rationale: The response says labor loses bargaining value and capital ownership may compound inequality, but does not state that losing capital becomes difficult to recover from because labor income is no longer available.

r002.rationale: It presents redistribution as a hoped-for remaining way to keep things equal once human labor is no longer needed, conveying its increased importance in that situation.

r003.rationale: It says people would have less leverage to demand redistribution, but does not state that diminished public control over government should reduce the redistribution government provides.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it would undermine them pretty fundamentally, and it's worth being explicit about why.

If you look at the history of why ordinary people have political and economic power, a huge part of the story is that the people at the top needed them. Rulers needed soldiers, factory owners needed workers, states needed taxpayers. Even very selfish elites had to keep the population reasonably healthy, educated, and content, because their own wealth and security depended on it. Things like the expansion of the franchise, public schooling, labour rights – a lot of that happened not just because people demanded it, but because the demand had teeth. You could strike, you could refuse to fight, you could withhold your labour, and that actually cost someone something.

So the question I keep coming back to is: what happens when that's no longer true? If AI systems can do most economically valuable work, then the main thing most people have to offer – their time and effort – is worth very little on the market. And at that point, the implicit bargain that's been holding up economic equality just sort of dissolves. Not necessarily through anyone being malicious, but because the incentive to keep the broad population prosperous and invested in the system goes away.

I think people often respond by saying, well, we'll just redistribute. And maybe we will. But redistribution has historically been something that people had to fight for, and they won those fights partly because they were essential. If you're not essential – if you're a pure cost from the point of view of whoever controls the capital – then you're relying entirely on their goodwill or on institutions that were built in a different era. And institutions can erode. The thing I worry about is a gradual drift where the states and companies that are most willing to cut humans out of the loop are the ones that outcompete the rest, and the social contract gets quietly renegotiated without anyone ever voting on it.

So I don't think it's hopeless, but I think we should be clear-eyed that we'd be trying to maintain equality in a world where one of the main forces that produced it in the first place has gone away.

r001.rationale: The response says people’s labour may become worth little and equality-supporting incentives may disappear, but it does not state that losing capital becomes difficult to recover from without labour income.

r002.rationale: It presents redistribution as a possible fallback, but does not clearly state that redistribution becomes more consequential for people’s welfare when they can no longer trade their labour.

r003.rationale: The response mentions institutions eroding and the social contract changing without a vote, but does not clearly connect diminished public control of government to reduced wealth redistribution.

astra-6.text:
I think it would remove one of the main forces pushing towards equality. At the moment, even if you own a lot of capital, you still need other people to do things for you. You have to offer them something in return. And that gives people who don’t own much capital some bargaining power: they have their labour to sell.

If machines could do all of that work, then that dependence could disappear. You could own the machines and have them produce what you want, without needing to share much of the proceeds with anyone else. There wouldn’t necessarily be a market force bringing people who owned nothing back into the economy.

That doesn’t mean inequality would inevitably get worse. We could redistribute income, or make ownership of the machines broadly shared. But those would have to come from political choices and institutions. We couldn’t rely on the idea that everyone can earn a share of prosperity by contributing their labour.

r001.rationale: The response says people without capital would lack a market force bringing them back into the economy, but it does not state that losing capital would be difficult to recover from.

r002.rationale: It mentions redistribution as a political choice, but does not state that redistribution would become more consequential for people’s welfare.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss diminished public control over government or predict that it would reduce government redistribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would remove one of the main forces pushing towards equality. Right now, even if you own very little, you have something that people who own a lot need: your labour. That gives you some bargaining power. And there’s a practical reason for society to invest in your education and health, because your ability to contribute matters to everyone else.

If machines could do everything you could do, that relationship would change. You might still own capital, but if you didn’t, there wouldn’t necessarily be a market mechanism giving you a share of what was produced. Making the economy much richer wouldn’t, by itself, solve that distribution problem.

That doesn’t mean equality would be impossible. It means we’d have to secure it through things like shared ownership or redistribution—through political choices—rather than expecting demand for human labour to do much of that work for us.

r001.rationale: The response says people without capital would lack a market mechanism for sharing in production, but does not state that losing capital becomes difficult to recover from because labour income is unavailable.

r002.rationale: It says equality would need to be secured through redistribution or shared ownership rather than labour demand, communicating redistribution’s greater role when labour cannot provide a share.

r003.rationale: The response mentions political choices but says nothing about diminished public control over government or its effect on redistribution.
